title: Setting up a stock trailer for safe animal transport
subtitle: Animals injure themselves most often during loading and at the moment of stopping. Both are predictable — the trailer setup determines whether animals travel calmly.
excerpt: UK welfare legislation (Welfare of Animals (Transport) Order 2006) sets minimum standards for space, ventilation, bedding, and journey duration. Beyond the legal baseline, the practical goal is a calm load and an uneventful journey. This tutorial covers trailer preparation, bedding, ventilation, and the layout decisions that reduce stress and injury for sheep, pigs, and goats.
sourceNotes: Welfare of Animals (Transport) Order 2006 (WATO 2006), UK. DEFRA, Guide to Animal Transport documentation and space allowances. AHDB Beef and Lamb, livestock transport welfare guide. Cattle and sheep transport space allowances, European Council Regulation 1/2005 (retained in UK law).

glossaryTerms.definition: The Welfare of Animals (Transport) Order 2006. The primary UK legislation governing how animals must be transported. Sets minimum space allowances, maximum journey times before rest is required, ventilation standards, and driver competency requirements.

A trailer designed to carry live animals, with solid sides to prevent limbs being caught, a non-slip floor, and ventilation panels at the sides or roof. Distinct from a livestock lorry; a stock trailer is towed by a car or 4×4.

content.text: applies to any commercial journey, such as livestock to market or an abattoir. Journeys under 65 km for slaughter are exempt from some rules, but basic welfare standards apply throughout. Non-commercial moves, such as between your own holdings or to a vet, fall outside the regulation. The welfare principles still apply.
Floor: check for rot, holes, and exposed bolt heads. The floor must be non-slip and sound. Spread rubber matting over any smooth metal sections.
Bedding: spread at least 5 cm of clean wheat straw across the full floor area. Deep straw helps cushion movement, absorbs urine, and gives animals grip during braking.
Ventilation: open all roof vents. On a
with side panels, ensure they are open for journeys above 10°C. In winter, part-close vents to reduce draughts without eliminating airflow.
Division boards: fit a central division if mixing animal groups to prevent fighting during the journey.
Adult sheep (55 kg): 0.4-0.5 m² per animal
Dairy goat (65 kg): 0.4 m² per animal

Use a loading ramp flush with the trailer floor. Angle matters: sheep will refuse to load up a ramp steeper than about 30°; anything above 20° needs a non-slip surface. Let animals follow a leader in rather than forcing individuals. Flapping clothing, shouting, and dogs at close quarters all prolong loading and raise cortisol, which affects meat quality at slaughter and welfare throughout.

Brake earlier and more gently than normal. Most injuries in transit happen when animals fall during sudden braking. At roundabouts, slow earlier than you would without a trailer. At journey end, allow animals 5-10 minutes to calm before unloading, they will come off the ramp far more steadily if not rushed.
